title: Intuition behind Analyzing Likelihood Shapes through Contours and Hessians
text:
When working with likelihood-based models, it is often useful to first form a rough picture of the likelihood surface before choosing an optimization or sampling method. Contour plots and Hessians provide two complementary views of this shape: contours show how likelihood varies across directions, while Hessians summarize local curvature at a point.
Throughout this post, contour plots refer to level sets of the likelihood function
\(f(y;\theta)\) as a function of the parameter vector \(\theta\). For visualization, \(\theta\) is restricted to two dimensions, even though the underlying parameter space is typically higher-dimensional.
A simple reference case is the round bowl. The contour lines are closed and nearly circular. Moving away from the center produces similar changes in the likelihood in all directions. No direction appears noticeably flatter than others.

When the parameters are highly correlated, the contour will be dense along the line \(\theta_1 \approx \alpha \theta_2\). In this case, contours become elongated and rotated, forming an elliptical bowl. The likelihood still decreases in all directions, but at different rates depending on direction. Some directions are flatter than others, though none are close to flat.

With stronger anisotropy, the contours stretch further and form a long, narrow corridor. The likelihood changes rapidly when moving across the corridor, while changes along the corridor are much slower. This type of shape is commonly referred to as a ridge.

These visual differences correspond to differences in local curvature, which are summarized by the Hessian matrix. The Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameters, evaluated at a point. Its eigenvalues describe curvature along orthogonal principal directions.
For example, a Hessian of the form
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
-50 & 10 \\
10 & -45
\end{pmatrix}
\]
has eigenvalues of comparable magnitude. Both principal directions exhibit similar curvature, which corresponds to the roughly circular contours above.
Increasing the off-diagonal terms produces stronger directional imbalance,
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
-50 & 20 \\
20 & -50
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here, one direction is flatter than the other, consistent with elongated but still well-behaved contours.
In a ridge-like case, the imbalance becomes extreme. A matrix such as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
-50 & 49 \\
49 & -50
\end{pmatrix}
\]
has eigenvalues that differ by orders of magnitude. For instance, one eigenvalue may be on the order of \(100\), while the other is close to \(0.1\). This indicates strong curvature in one direction and an almost flat direction in another, matching the narrow corridor seen in the contour plot.
The separation between eigenvalues is often summarized by the condition number,
\[
\kappa = \frac{|\lambda_{\max}|}{|\lambda_{\min}|}.
\]
Large values correspond to highly uneven curvature. By contrast, the determinant only reflects the product of curvatures across directions: it becomes small when at least one direction is nearly flat, but it does not distinguish a ridge from a uniformly rescaled surface.
Contour plots and Hessians provide a compact way to form a basic picture of likelihood shape. Contours show how likelihood changes across directions in parameter space, while Hessians quantify this behavior locally at a point. Over time, reading these two objects side by side becomes a practical way to anticipate how different numerical methods are likely to behave.

title: Introduction to Machine Learning: Gradient Descent and Neural Networks
text:
To understand machine learning, one must have a basic understanding of optimization. In a learning problem, a loss function is specified to evaluate estimation accuracy, and the goal of optimization is to minimize this loss. Specifically, a loss function assigns a scalar value to model predictions as a quantitative measure of estimation error. Common examples include:
Mean Squared Error (MSE): \[L_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat y_i - y_i)^2\]
Mean Absolute Error (MAE): \[L_{\text{MAE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |\hat y_i - y_i\]
For binary classification, cross-entropy is commonly used: \[L_{\text{CE}} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i\log \hat p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat p_i)\right]\]
Below is an example of the loss function of MSE.
import numpy as np 

y_true = np.array([10,20,30])
y_pred = np.array([12,18,27])

loss = np.mean((y_true-y_pred)**2 )
print(loss)
Once a loss function is specified, the next question is how to minimize it. This is handled by optimization algorithms. We introduce the most fundamental algorithm - gradient descent here.
For a differentiable function, the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. Minimization therefore proceeds by updating parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient. The step size of each update is controlled by the learning rate, whereas an excessively large learning rate may cause overshooting and divergence, and an excessively small learning rate leads to slow convergence.
Below is an example of gradient descent for a linear regression \(\hat y = w x\) with loss \(L = (y_{\text{true}} - wx)^2\). The gradient with respect to \(w\) is \({\partial L}/{\partial w} = -2x (y_{\text{true}} - wx)\). Change the learning rate in the code below to see how it affects the optimization process. (It is generally good around 0.004. I have to change from Python to ObservableJS to make it interactive here.)

viewof learning_rate = Inputs.range([0.0001, 0.05], {step: 0.0005, value: 0.001, label: "learning rate"})







"Good Day Reader!🥰 Select your learning rate here👆"







x = 10;
y_true = 100;
w0 = 8;

w = w0;

outputs = {
  let w = w0;
  let results = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    let y_pred = w * x;
    let gradient = -2 * x * (y_true - y_pred);
    w = w - learning_rate * gradient;
    results.push(`iteration ${i+1}: current prediction ${y_pred.toFixed(2)}, next w ${w.toFixed(2)}`);
  }
  return results;
}

html`<ul>${outputs.map(item => html`<li>${item}</li>`)}</ul>`











































So far, the model is a si mple linear regression. Next, we upgrade this regression model to a neural network. A neural network contains an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Each layer applies a linear transformation followed by an activation function.
For a generic layer,
\[z = W x + b,\quad h = \phi(z)\],
where \(\phi(\cdot)\) denotes an activation function. Common choices include ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh. ReLU preserves positive inputs and truncates negative ones. Sigmoid and tanh map real-valued inputs into bounded intervals.
ReLU: \(\phi(z) = \max(0, z)\). Sigmoid:\(\phi(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\). Tanh:\(\phi(z) = \frac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{e^{z} + e^{-z}}\). Softmax (for vector-valued input \(z\)):\(\phi(z_j) = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}}\).
All these activation functions introduce nonlinearity。 Without activation functions, stacking multiple layers would still result in a linear model. Like in linear regression, we can also use gradient descent to optimize the parameters of a neural network. The gradients can be computed using backpropagation, which applies the chain rule of calculus to propagate gradients from the output layer back to the input layer. For example, we consider a neural network with 2 hidden layers. The input \(x\) is transformed through the first hidden layer to produce \(h_1\), then through the second hidden layer to produce \(h_2\), and finally to the output \(y\).
Forward:
\[\begin{aligned}
z_{1,i} &= W_1 x_i + b_1, \\
h_{1,i} &= \mathrm{ReLU}(z_{1,i}), \\
z_{2,i} &= W_2 h_{1,i} + b_2, \\
h_{2,i} &= \mathrm{ReLU}(z_{2,i}), \\
\hat{y}_i &= W_3 h_{2,i} + b_3.
\end{aligned}\]
By the chain rule, backpropagation gives: \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_1}
=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat y}
\cdot
\frac{\partial \hat y}{\partial h_2}
\cdot
\frac{\partial h_2}{\partial z_2}
\cdot
\frac{\partial z_2}{\partial h_1}
\cdot
\frac{\partial h_1}{\partial z_1}
\cdot
\frac{\partial z_1}{\partial W_1}.\]The goal is still to minimize the MSE, \(L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat y_i - y_i)^2\). For this network, the loss is differentiable with respect to all parameters, so gradients can be written in closed form using the chain rule. Specifically, for ReLu, the derivative is defined in a piecewise manner,
\[
\frac{d}{dz}\mathrm{ReLU}(z) =
\begin{cases}
1, & z > 0, \\
0, & z < 0,
\end{cases}
\]
and a subgradient at ( z=0 ) is typically chosen by convention. This leads to the indicator term ( (z>0) ) appearing in the gradients.
We analytically write out the gradients for all parameters below.
\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_3}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat y_i - y_i)\, h_{2,i}^T\),
\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_3}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat y_i - y_i)\),
\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_2}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(\hat y_i - y_i)\,
W_3\,

(\hat y_i - y_i)\,

=

title: A Guide to Distinguishing Tail Classes: Single Big Jumps
text:
A fundamental distinction in probability theory and econometrics is whether a distribution possesses a moment generating function (MGF).
Let
\[
M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]
\]
denote the MGF of a random variable \(X\).
A distribution \(F\) is called heavy-tailed if
\[
M_X(t) = \infty, \qquad \forall t > 0
\]
In contrast, if there exists some \(t>0\) such that
\[
M_X(t) < \infty,
\]
the distribution is said to be light-tailed.
This criterion acts as a natural “death line”: once the MGF ceases to exist, classical exponential large-deviation tools break down, and extreme outcomes become fundamentally more likely.

A fundamental distinction in probability theory and econometrics is whether a distribution possesses a moment generating function (MGF).
Let
\[
M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]
\]
denote the MGF of a random variable \(X\).
A distribution \(F\) is called heavy-tailed if
\[
M_X(t) = \infty, \qquad \forall t > 0
\]
In contrast, if there exists some \(t>0\) such that
\[
M_X(t) < \infty,
\]
the distribution is said to be light-tailed.
This criterion acts as a natural “death line”: once the MGF ceases to exist, classical exponential large-deviation tools break down, and extreme outcomes become fundamentally more likely.

title: A Guide to Distinguishing Tail Classes: Single Big Jumps
text:
2. The Hierarchy of Heavy Tails
Heavy-tailed distributions themselves form a structured hierarchy.
A commonly used nesting is
\[
\text{Regularly Varying}
\subset
\text{Subexponential}
\subset
\text{Long-tailed}
\subset
\text{Heavy-tailed}.
\]
Each step corresponds to progressively weaker assumptions about how slowly the tail decays.


2.1 Long-tailed distributions
A distribution belongs to the long-tailed class if
\[
\frac{\bar F(x+y)}{\bar F(x)} \to 1
\quad \text{as } x \to \infty
\]
for every fixed \(y\), where
\[
\bar F(x) = P(X>x)
\]
is the survival function.
Intuitively, adding a fixed constant \(y\) barely changes the tail probability when \(x\) is large.



2.2 Subexponential distributions and the “Single Big Jump”
A central subclass of heavy tails is the subexponential class, defined by
\[
\overline{F^{*2}}(x) \sim 2\bar F(x),
\quad x \to \infty.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
P(X_1 + X_2 > x) \sim 2P(X > x)
\]
for independent copies \(X_1, X_2\).
This property leads to the Single Big Jump Principle:

When a sum of subexponential variables becomes extremely large, it is typically caused by one extreme observation, rather than by the accumulation of many moderate values.




2.3 Regular variation (power-law tails)
The most widely studied heavy tails are regularly varying tails, characterized by
\[
\frac{\bar F(tx)}{\bar F(x)} \to t^{-\alpha},
\quad t>0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\bar F(x) = x^{-\alpha} L(x),
\]
where \(L(x)\) is a slowly varying function.
Regular variation provides a tractable mathematical structure and plays a central role in extreme value theory and financial tail modeling.

title: A Guide to Distinguishing Tail Classes: Single Big Jumps
text:
3. Light Tails: The “Conspiracy of Smalls”
Light-tailed distributions behave very differently from heavy-tailed ones.
For light tails, the probability of producing one extremely large observation is exponentially small. As a result, extreme sums typically arise through the combined effect of multiple moderately large values, rather than a single outlier.
For example, suppose
\[
f(x) \propto e^{-x^2}.
\]
To produce a sum of \(10\):

Single jump: \((10 + 0)\) gives probability \(\propto e^{-100}\)
Two moderate values: \((5 + 5)\) gives probability \(\propto e^{-50}\)

Since \(e^{-50} \gg e^{-100}\), the second scenario dominates.
This phenomenon explains why Gaussian-type distributions do not satisfy the subexponential property.

title: A Guide to Distinguishing Tail Classes: Single Big Jumps
text:
4. Summary of Tail Classes








Class
Mathematical Criterion
Typical Examples




Light-tailed
\(M_X(t)<\infty\) for some \(t>0\)
Normal, Exponential


Heavy-tailed
\(M_X(t)=\infty\) for all \(t>0\)
Lognormal, Pareto


Long-tailed
\(\bar F(x+y)/\bar F(x)\to1\)
Pareto, Lognormal


Subexponential
\(\overline{F^{*2}}(x)/\bar F(x)\to2\)
Pareto, Lognormal


Regularly varying
\(\bar F(tx)/\bar F(x)\to t^{-\alpha}\)
Pareto, Student-t

title: A Guide to Distinguishing Tail Classes: Single Big Jumps
text:
5. Conclusion
Tail behavior determines how extreme events arise.

In light-tailed environments, extreme outcomes result from a conspiracy of many moderate deviations.
In subexponential environments, extremes are dominated by a single big jump.

Understanding which regime a model belongs to is crucial for applications ranging from risk management to econometric modeling of financial volatility.
